title: The Claude Delusion
lede: A personal essay argues that successful tech figures overrate AI because they overrate themselves, using Bill Gates's account of judging OpenAI and Claude as its main example.

points: The author says success, often largely luck, leads tech leaders to assume expertise well outside their field.
Gates testing GPT on AP biology questions he wrote himself is cited as overconfidence in a domain he does not practise.
Gates calling Claude's coding as good as his own, and therefore superhuman, is read as ego rather than evidence.
The essay links this mindset to both AI doom and utopian narratives, and to agent talk that shifts responsibility away from builders.

points.text: Most top comments reject the essay's take on Gates, arguing that a strong programmer who spent years evaluating engineers is well placed to judge coding models.
Commenters see a contradiction: the essay faults Gates for judging biology outside his field, then dismisses him in coding, where he is an expert.
Some side with the author, citing Microsoft's slow start on the internet, while a reply points to Gates's 1995 Internet Tidal Wave memo.
Several cite firsthand experience, such as a veteran reverse engineer who says Claude Code cracked a hard proprietary encoding problem.
